# Training And Checkpoints

`rf.Model` runs fitting, validation, testing, and batched prediction through
Lightning internally. Pass a data module and configure execution on the model
methods. Direct use of `lit.Trainer` remains available for framework tooling.

To learn from unlabeled records and then adapt to a labeled task, follow
[Pretraining And Fine-Tuning](pretraining.qmd).

## Fit A Model

Start with a constructed model and independent Arrow `train_table` and
`validation_table` inputs. The model needs at least one reconstruction
objective, such as `mask=True` on a label. An unconfigured optimizer defaults
to AdamW with a learning rate of `1e-3`.

```python
import relflow as rf

datamodule = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    model=model,
    train=train_table,
    validate=validation_table,
)
model.fit(datamodule, max_epochs=50, checkpoint_dir="checkpoints/customer")
```

For eager Polars frames, use `rf.PolarsDataModule(model=model,
train=train_frame, validate=validation_frame)`. It converts the frames to Arrow
at ingress. See [Data Modules](data-modules.qmd) for source and split choices.

Pass an optimizer instance or a factory receiving the model, either through
`Model(optimizer=...)` or `model.optimizer`. A factory collects the current
parameters when Lightning configures optimization. `scheduler` accepts a
scheduler, a Lightning scheduler configuration, or a factory receiving
`(model, optimizer)`.

Early stopping and rollback are enabled by default. Both monitor `loss/validate`
in `min` mode; patience is ten validation checks and `min_delta` is zero. Full
best and last checkpoints are saved. Without `checkpoint_dir`, the run uses a
unique directory under `default_root_dir/checkpoints`. Fitting restores the best
model state, including schema, vocabularies, and normalizers, before returning
the model. Read [Evaluation](evaluation.qmd) before choosing a monitor.

Set `early_stopping=False` or `rollback=False` to disable either policy. Train-only
fitting disables both or explicitly chooses a training monitor such as
`loss/train`. Each policy also accepts a configured `rf.EarlyStopping` or
`rf.RollbackCheckpoint` callback. Policy callbacks in `callbacks` replace their
automatic defaults; other Lightning callbacks run alongside the built-ins.

## Report Progress And Validate

`Model.track` uses Lightning's native logging: training metrics are available
per step and as epoch aggregates. `log_every_n_steps`, defaulting to 50, controls
how often attached loggers receive step metrics. Step values describe the latest
batch, rather than an average over that interval. With gradient accumulation,
logging follows optimizer updates. Set `log_every_n_steps=0` to disable step
emission while keeping epoch logging.

Lightning appends `_step` and `_epoch` to training metric names in logger output,
such as `loss/train_step` and `loss/train_epoch`. The unsuffixed `loss/train`
remains available to callbacks; `loss/validate` remains the default checkpoint
and early-stopping monitor. More frequent logging does not run validation, save
checkpoints, change patience, or advance schedulers. See
[Evaluation](evaluation.qmd) for metric definitions.

```python
model.fit(datamodule, logger=application_logger, log_every_n_steps=50)
```

For learning-rate logging, add Lightning's `LearningRateMonitor` to `callbacks`.

Validation normally runs at the end of each epoch. To evaluate long training
streams more frequently, supply an integer `val_check_interval` in **training
batches**. With `check_val_every_n_epoch=None`, the interval continues across
epoch boundaries:

```python
model.fit(
    datamodule,
    logger=application_logger,
    log_every_n_steps=50,
    val_check_interval=1_000,
    check_val_every_n_epoch=None,
)
```

Early stopping and best-checkpoint selection follow validation. Patience counts
validation checks with no improvement, so increasing validation frequency can
stop training sooner. Keep the held-out observations and masking policy
consistent across checks. Checkpoint filenames include both epoch and optimizer
step to distinguish evaluations within one epoch. Make sure a configured fit
runs long enough to reach validation when its selection policies require it.

All loops process their configured splits without automatic time or batch caps.
Use explicit batch limits for smoke tests or deliberate sampling:

```python
model.fit(datamodule, max_epochs=1, limit_train_batches=10, limit_val_batches=2)
model.validate(datamodule, limit_val_batches=100)
model.test(datamodule, limit_test_batches=100)
```

Use integer batch counts for Arrow iterable loaders. Data-module sampling and
`epoch_size` remain explicit data-selection choices. Lightning's `max_time` sets
a budget for the whole fit. `fast_dev_run=True` skips automatic early stopping
and rollback for Lightning's single-pass diagnostic run.

## Choose The Loop

| Call | Required data split | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `model.fit(datamodule)` | `train` and, for the default policies, `validate` | Optimize and restore the best model. |
| `model.validate(datamodule)` | `validate` | Return one metric dictionary per loader. |
| `model.test(datamodule)` | `test` | Return held-out metrics per loader. |
| `model.predict(datamodule=...)` | `predict` | Collect an Arrow table on one device or stream with a Writer. |

Stages also control masking and field-owned learning, such as vocabulary and
normalizer updates. Use the corresponding split rather than repurposing a
training loader for inference. For bounded requests, the separate
`model.predict(observations)` convenience returns an Arrow table without a
Trainer; see [Prediction Output](prediction-output.qmd).

Hardware defaults to `accelerator="auto"`, `devices="auto"`, DDP for multiple
devices or nodes, and BF16 mixed precision when all selected devices support it.
Otherwise precision is FP32. Supply explicit `accelerator`, `devices`,
`precision`, or `strategy` to override these choices. Other Trainer arguments
pass through; `callbacks` works on all four loops. `batch_size` updates the one
model-owned batch size. relflow installs its required callbacks automatically.
Compile
selected model regions before the loop with `model.compile()` if desired;
[Performance](performance.qmd) describes exactly what this compiles.

## Local Distributed Training

For CPU distributed training on one Mac, if Gloo aborts with
`uv_accept: invalid argument`, select the loopback interface before launching
your training script:

```bash
GLOO_SOCKET_IFNAME=lo0 uv run python train.py
```

This keeps communication between local ranks on macOS's loopback interface.
For training across machines, select a network interface reachable from every
rank. PyTorch documents this setting under
[Gloo network interface configuration](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/distributed.html#choosing-the-network-interface-to-use).

## Save And Load

Use a relflow artifact to retain the schema and learned model state:

```python
model.save("artifacts/customer.rf")
loaded = rf.Model.load("artifacts/customer.rf")
predictions = loaded.predict(observations)
```

The artifact contains the state dictionary, schema, batch size, and producing
relflow version. State includes field-owned buffers such as vocabularies and
normalizers. `load` constructs the model on CPU. Move it to the intended device
for direct inference; Lightning owns placement when using its loops.

Schemas now use an anonymous root at `/` and slash-prefixed child addresses.
Artifacts from the former named-root format are not compatible and are rejected
on load. New artifacts omit the root name and preserve child names as before.

A `Model.save` artifact does not contain optimizer or scheduler state, Trainer
progress, data sources, or processor configuration. Supply those explicitly
when fitting a loaded model. Compilation is transient and must be requested
again after loading.

## Resume Training

The default rollback callback saves best and last full checkpoints at its
validation/epoch checkpoints. The best model is selected for its validation
score; the last checkpoint preserves the most recent state saved by that
callback. For recovery between validation checks, attach a separate unmonitored
checkpoint callback:

```python
from lightning.pytorch.callbacks import ModelCheckpoint

recovery = ModelCheckpoint(
    dirpath="checkpoints/recovery",
    filename="step-{step}",
    monitor=None,
    every_n_train_steps=1_000,
    save_top_k=1,
    save_last=True,
)
model.fit(datamodule, callbacks=[recovery])
```

The recovery checkpoint contains optimizer and scheduler state. Its step
schedule does not select the best model using a previous validation score;
the built-in rollback callback continues to select from fresh validation checks.

Use a full Lightning checkpoint to resume optimizer/scheduler state and loop
progress. Recreate the runtime configuration and pass the checkpoint to `fit`:

```python
resumed = rf.Model.load("checkpoints/recovery/last.ckpt")
resumed.optimizer = rf.adamw(learning_rate=1e-3)
resume_data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    model=resumed,
    train=train_table,
    validate=validation_table,
)
resumed.fit(
    resume_data,
    max_epochs=100,
    ckpt_path="checkpoints/recovery/last.ckpt",
)
```

Recreate any scheduler and keep optimizer configuration consistent with the
saved run. `rf.Model.load` restores model state; the `ckpt_path` argument is
what tells Lightning to resume training state.

Another `fit` call without `ckpt_path` starts a new optimizer run from the current
model state. Use the best full checkpoint to continue with optimizer and
scheduler state matching the restored best model. After rollback, construct a
new optimizer instance or supply a factory; factories bind the current graph.
